    NECESSITY FOR THE BELL COUNTY                     §
    EAST SWITCH TO BIG HILL SUBSTATION                §
    765-KV TRANSMISSION LINE PROJECT IN               §
    BELL, BURNET, CONCHO, CORYELL,                    §
    LAMPASAS,       LLANO,      MASON,                §
    MCCULLOCH, MENARD, MILAM, MILLS,                  §
    SAN SABA, SCHLEICHER, TOM GREEN,                  §
    AND WILLIAMSON COUNTIES                           §

                     FLEMING SPRINGS RANCH LAND COMPANY, LLC’S
                             INITIAL POST HEARING BRIEF

TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:

          Intervenor Fleming Springs Ranch Land Company, LLC (“Fleming Springs”), owner of

the Fleming Springs Ranch, files this Initial Post Hearing Brief, and respectfully shows:

I.        Introduction

          The Fleming Springs Ranch is located in San Saba County, Texas, 4–5 miles east of the

town of San Saba, on the south side of Highway 190. It would be affected by any route using

proposed Links U5 and U6, which are part of the network of far northern links added to this project

after the opportunity for public involvement had passed. The Legislature requires that community

values be considered in these proceedings.1 But the study area community, writ large, was not

given the opportunity to consider and provide input on these late-added U-Links before the

Application was filed. Indeed, Applicant’s evidence suggests that the northern U-Links were

added at the urging of community members to the south, who were given the opportunity to


1
    PURA, §37.056(c)(4)(A).

FLEMING SPRINGS INITIAL BRIEF                                                               PAGE 1
 provide public input. As a consequence, any route utilizing any of these U-Links would fly in the

face of community values; the concept cannot be allowed to mean “go put it in my neighbor’s

yard, who was not given the opportunity to weigh in.”

         The Fleming Springs Ranch is an historical ranch located on a network of springs that feed

into the San Saba River and, ultimately, the Colorado River. 2 Humans have lived in and around

this location for 14,000 years. 3 More recently, the ranch’s main house was built in 1856 to

capitalize on these springs, and the ranch has been painstakingly maintained since. A route using

the northern U-Links in this case, in addition to impacting Fleming Springs Ranch, would also

have a detrimental impact on the ranch’s neighbors in the San Saba area. Such a route would

impact the community of San Saba and the municipal water the community greatly depends on,

including Simpson Creek, Fleming Springs Branch, and Barnett Springs Creek, which feed the

San Saba and Colorado Rivers.4 The proposed U5 and U6 structures would shadow the historic

county seat community and impede the few roads in and around the community and its landowners

during construction. Such a route would impact indigenous sites like 5 Mile Hill, which is partially

located on the Fleming Springs Ranch south of HWY 190 and was used by the Comanche to signal

other tribal sites in distant locations.5

        Fleming Springs believes that this entire project should be avoided. Nonetheless, Fleming

Springs supports Applicants’ best-meets route, Route 894, because, on balance, it is the route that

most appropriately satisfies the applicable routing criteria. Route 894 performs best in terms of

prudent avoidance while also resulting in comparatively lower environmental impact. At the same

FLEMING SPRINGS INITIAL BRIEF                                                               PAGE 2
 time, Route 894 maintains costs that are reasonable relative to the full range of route alternatives.

Fleming Springs also has no objection to the Staff Route, Route 487.

        Fleming Springs opposes all routes that utilize Links U5 and U6. These Northern Links

were added late to this project. They were not identified on any of Applicants’ preliminary maps,

and they were not analyzed or discussed at any of the public involvement meetings before the

Application was filed. While communities to the south of San Saba hosted public involvement

meetings, none was held in San Saba. As a consequence, influential landowners in and around the

southern portion of the study area had the opportunity to mobilize and prepare for this proceeding

months before landowners in the San Saba area, like Fleming Springs, who did not learn they were

potentially in the crosshairs until the Application was filed. This is not how community values

and public participation are supposed to work.

        One such group of intervenors, whose prefiled testimony confirms their experts were

analyzing routes before the Northern U-Routes were even on the map, proposes Route 392. 6 Route

392’s sole claimed advantage is that it crosses the Colorado River at late-added Link U3, which

has the alleged benefit of paralleling an existing 17.25-mile transmission line. The virtues of that

paralleling are debatable; the existing line is a much older line with a materially smaller impact

than the line at issue in this Docket. But in virtually every other metric, Route 894 is superior.

894 is shorter, it is cheaper, it affects fewer habitable structures, and it traverses less sensitive

riparian habitat.

        As noted, and as will be explained in more detail below, the modest benefit of an additional

12 miles of paralleling an older, smaller existing transmission line at a single river crossing must

be weighed against Route 392’s $34 million in additional estimated costs and 51 more habitable

Rhodes, Ph.D.) at 18.

FLEMING SPRINGS INITIAL BRIEF                                                                           PAGE 3
 structures, as compared to route 894. Fleming Springs suggests that this is not a reasonable

tradeoff for the Commission to endorse, if the Commission considers routes using the U-Links at

all (which it should not).

II.     Summary of Prefiled Testimony

        A.       Fleming Springs Ranch Land Company, LLC

        Dawn Laurel - Jones. Ms. Jones testified as a member of Fleming Springs Ranch Land

Company, LLC, which owns the Fleming Springs Ranch. 7 Ms. Jones’s testimony highlighted the

property’s unique historical and geological features, including an original main house located atop

Fleming Springs Branch, which was commissioned by Jeremiah Fleming in 1856 and constructed

by Bavarian stonemasons using locally sourced Ellenburger outcropping limestone.8

Archaeological evidence and Native American artifacts discovered on the property demonstrate

that the area has been occupied for more than 14,000 years.

        Further, Ms. Jones’s testimony established the significant investments and stewardship

efforts made on the property, including the preservation of more than 16 varieties of oak trees, as

well as large mesquite and old-growth Ashe juniper. 9 Her testimony highlighted the cultivation of

a robust and healthy native white-tailed deer population through dedicated habitat preservation

efforts, along with the preservation of pronghorn milkweed, green milkweed, and butterfly weed

throughout the ranch in support of the threatened Monarch butterfly migration. 10

        Finally, Fleming Springs Ranch contains three important springs, Simpson Creek, Fleming

Springs Branch, and Barnett Creek, which are all part of the Ellenburger-San Saba and Marble

 Falls Aquifer.11 The Ellenburger-San Saba is a minor aquifer found in parts of 16 counties in the

Llano Uplift area of Central Texas.12 These Springs contribute essential baseflow to the San Saba

River and ultimately to the Colorado River, supporting agriculture, municipal water for the San

Saba community, and riparian and estuarine habitat systems. 13

        B.       Applicant

        As noted above, Joint Applicants identified Route 894 as the route that best meets all

applicable routing criteria.14

        C.       PUC Staff

        As noted above, PUC Staff identified Route 487 as the route that best meets all applicable

routing criteria.15

III.    Routing Analysis – Why Route 894 outperforms Route 392

        A more detailed analysis of the record evidence follows.

        A. Statutory Criteria

                  1. Community Values and Public Input; PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(A)

        PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(A) requires consideration of impacts of proposed transmission

facilities on community values. While “community values” are not formally defined by statute or

rule, the Commission has previously defined “community values” as: a shared appreciation of an

area or other natural or human resource by a national, regional, or local community. 16 Adverse

effects upon community values consist of those aspects of a Proposed Project that would

by a community.

         The PUC’s Order of Referral in this case also requires that the ALJs address principal

concerns expressed by community members at public meetings held by the Applicants. 17 Pre-

application public meetings are required by PUC rules.18 In this case, Applicants held three public

meetings, in June of 2025.19 A stated purpose of these meetings was to “Identify the values and

concerns of the public and community leaders.” 20 These meetings were held in Salado, Lampasas,

and Menard.21 The map used to provide notice of these public meetings did not indicate that the

U-Links were a possibility, and the community of San Saba (where no meeting was held), is only

barely on the map22 Excerpts from the public meeting map are below:

         At this point in the process, the U-Links were literally not on the map. Because no

preliminary link came within miles of San Saba or the Fleming Springs Ranch, notice of the public

meetings was not sent to Fleming Springs Ranch or to any landowners potentially affected by what

are now identified as the U-Links. Consideration of the U-Links would therefore violate PUC

procedural rules, which require notice of pre-Application public meetings to owners of land within

500 feet of the centerline of a transmission project greater than 230kV. 23

        Landowners who did receive notice of the public meetings were obviously given the

opportunity to participate, and they (not unreasonably) took advantage of it. The intervenor group

who now strongly advocates for a route that would use Link U3 had engaged and hired expert

witnesses by the Fall of 2025, i.e. within months of the public meetings, and months before any

maps showing what are now the U-Links were released. 24 Fleming Springs does not suggest that

there is anything wrong with a landowner hiring experts after the public notice maps were released.

Fleming Springs does suggest that it, and all San Saba area landowners, should have been given

that same opportunity.

        After the public meetings far to the south of San Saba, Applicants added the U-Links, which

would cut through the study area at its far northern edge, in and around the town of San Saba. 25

 This was done as a result of input received from the public meetings, 26 meetings to which affected

U-Link landowners were not invited. Fleming Springs acknowledges that landowners almost

never want enormous transmission lines on their property, but the playing field should be level.

The public involvement process was not intended to be a mechanism for noticed affected

landowners to band together to push the line onto property not given notice of the meeting.

Allowing the public involvement process to implement “NIMBY” decisionmaking subverts the

important purpose of the required process.

        A PFD recommending a route utilizing a U-Link cannot be based on any evidence of

community values, because the values of the community that would be affected by the U-Links

were not solicited or taken into account.

                  2. Recreational and Park Areas; PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(B)

        During the hearing on the merits, the parties engaged in extensive discussion concerning

the potential impact of the proposed transmission line on Colorado Bend State Park and Post Oak

Ridge State Park, both of which are located along the Colorado River. 27 Both State Parks are

significant resources and visited by thousands of Texans every year. Colorado Bend State Park, a

5,328-acre park along the Colorado River in San Saba County, features caves, canyon walls,

spring-fed creeks, Gorman Falls, and more than 35 miles of hiking trails. Directly across the river,

the newly established 3,118-acre Post Oak Ridge State Park was acquired through the voter-

approved Centennial Parks Conservation Fund.28 Together, the parks create an approximately

10,000-acre protected landscape along the Colorado River and represent one of the most

significant public land conservation expansions in Texas in recent decades.

         The proposed transmission line presents six different options for crossing the Colorado

River: J11, J22, J26, J31, U2, and U3.29 Two of these Links, Link J11 and Link J26, each pass

within the half-mile foreground visual zone of one or both state parks in the study area. 30

        Link J11 is located approximately 100 feet south of the northern boundary of Colorado

Bend State Park and crosses Colorado Park Road, the park’s primary entrance route. 31 This section

of roadway serves as the main access point to the park, including the location of the entrance and

fee booth.32

        Link J26 borders the southern edge of Post Oak Ridge State Park, placing it within the

park’s half-mile foreground visual zone.33 It also falls within the half-mile foreground visual zone

of an approximately 260-foot portion of the Spicewood Springs Trail, which runs along the

southern boundary of Colorado Bend State Park. 34

        Avoiding Links J11 and J26 should be a priority for the Commission. In this context, Route

894 stands out as a particularly prudent alternative, as it achieves the project’s objectives without

relying on either of these links.

        Furthermore, the EA data confirms that Route 894 crosses zero miles of right-of-way

within the foreground visual zone of any park or recreation area. While Route 392 also avoids both

Links J11 and J26, the EA data shows that the Route places 0.73 miles of right-of-way within the

foreground visual zone of a park or recreational area.

data highlights a consistent trend in which Route 894 either matches or outperforms Route 392

across the key evaluation criteria.

                  3. Aesthetic and historical values; PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(C)
        The Lower Colorado River is internationally recognized for its unparalleled archaeological

resources, including habitation shelters and deeply stratified cultural deposits. 35 The Fleming

Springs Ranch Head Quarters was built in 1856 by Bavarian stone masons with local Ellenburger

limestone for Jeremiah Fleming, on top of the Fleming Springs Branch. Various Native American

artifacts have been found around the house and along the spring stretching to the San Saba River. 36

This structure is one of the few two story farmhouses ever built in this region during the mid to

late 1800’s.37

         The Legislature has charged the ALJ and the Commission with minimizing harm to these

irreplaceable assets by including their consideration under PURA §37.056(c)(4)(C). The

archaeological significance of the Lower Colorado River extends well beyond individual aesthetic

values, as these properties contain unique cultural resources that will continue to inform research

and understanding for generations.

        While several properties in the study area contain aesthetic and historical artifacts, the

Environmental Assessment data concerning cultural resource sites overwhelmingly favors Route

894 over Route 392.38

        Route 392 crosses 16 recorded cultural resource sites, compared to only 2 for Route 894.

Route 894 also has significantly fewer recorded cultural resources within 1,000 feet of the route

centerline, with only 12 compared to 47 for Route 392. 40 Under these criteria, Route 894 is far

superior to Route 392 in minimizing impacts to cultural resources.

                  4. Environmental integrity; PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(D)

        Fleming Springs provided extensive evidence of the property’s rich riparian ecosystem

along the Fleming Springs Branch, Simpson Creek, and Barnett Springs Creek, and various other

aquifer recharge zones characterized by limestone hills, pecan woodlands, and diverse

wildlife.41 The ranch has several varieties of pecan trees including Native Texas Pecans on or near

the Fleming Springs Branch. The ranch supports Little Bluestem, Texas Cup Grass, Sideoats

Grama, Big Bluestem, and Buffalo Grass. Fleming Springs Ranch supports diverse wildlife,

including white-tailed deer, wild turkey, bobwhite quail, coyotes, bobcats, cougars, and various

reptiles, along with numerous bird species such as vireos, wrens, tanagers, owls, and raptors.

Migratory species, including Painted Buntings, Gray Catbirds, Yellow-billed Cuckoos, Vermilion

Flycatchers, and Black-bellied Whistling Ducks, rely on the ranch’s riparian areas, springs, and

recharge zones as critical stopover habitat along the Central Flyway. 42

         Supporters of Route 392 point to its Colorado River crossing at Link U3, where it parallels

an existing transmission line, as the decisive reason the Commission should select Route 392.43

This ignores the environmental impact that Link U3 would have on the Colorado River. At the

hearing, there was significant discussion about Ecological Significant Stream Segment (ESSS)

designations, assigned by the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department. 44 The ESSS designation

identifies river and stream segments of particular ecological importance based on biological

function, hydrologic function, riparian conservation areas, high water quality and exceptional

aquatic life, and the presence of threatened or endangered species. 45

         Links U3, U2, and J11 are the three northernmost proposed Colorado River crossings

within the Study Area, and all three traverse the designated ESSS portion of the river, unlike the

southern crossings, which are not designated ESSS.46 This data shows that selecting a Colorado

River crossing in this proceeding involves nuanced tradeoffs, requiring a balance between

environmental integrity and all other routing considerations.

        B. Commission Rule Criteria

                  1. Engineering Constraints; 16 TAC § 25.101(c)(3)(B)

        The Applicants assert that they do not anticipate material engineering constraints

associated with construction of the proposed alternative routes. However, the record also

demonstrates that the study area includes conditions that may present significant challenges. These

include the complexity and potential costs associated with construction crossing the Colorado

River which is a crossing that every proposed route in this proceeding must address in some form.

 All of the northern routes that utilize the U-links are longer routes which would only further

complicate the engineering challenges inherent in spanning a major waterway such as the Colorado

River.

                  2. Costs; 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B)

         The estimated transmission line project costs range from approximately $2.032 billion for

Route 469 to $2.253 billion for Route 910.47 Route 894 has relatively low estimated cost, at

$2,076,387,000, placing it within 2.2 percent of the lowest cost alternative, Route 469. 48 Route

894 represents a reasonable tradeoff between cost and impact mitigation and cannot reasonably be

characterized as cost prohibitive, given that it is $24,102,730 below the average cost of all

alternative routes.49 Most notably, Route 894 is $34,299,000 cheaper than Route 392. 50 Testimony

at the hearing established that the cost of this project represents real expenses that will ultimately

be passed on to Texas ratepayers.

         Supporters of Route 392 argue that the $34,299,000 cost difference between Route 894 and

Route 392 reflects “false precision” given the preliminary nature of construction cost estimates. 51

Taking this to its logical conclusion, that argument would eliminate cost as a distinguishing factor

in every transmission line proceeding in Texas, since all preliminary estimates inherently involve

some uncertainty.

         The cost estimates for this project were prepared using the same methodology and applied

uniformly across all 122 filed routes. The cost contingency affects all routes proportionally; it

does not selectively impact Route 392’s costs but not Route 894’s. As expert Brian C. Andrews

selective.52 Any potential increase in costs, whether due to tariffs, material escalation, or

        Longer routes are going to be more expensive. Their contingencies are proportionate to

their increased costs, and their uncertainties are proportionate to their increased costs. Route 392

is almost 6 miles longer than Route 894.


                  3. Paralleling; 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B)(i)-(iii) Criteria

        Under 16 TAC Section 25.101(b)(3)(B), the Commission considers the extent to which a

proposed route parallels existing compatible rights of way, including transmission lines, roads,

highways, railways, and apparent property lines.

        Proponents of Route 392 focus on the route’s Colorado River crossing and its associated

paralleling performance at that location. Specifically, they argue that Route 392’s use of Link U3,

which crosses the Colorado River parallel to an existing transmission line, makes it the best

location to cross the River. This argument overstates the benefits of this paralleling, because the

paralleling in question only supports Link U3 if the existing line which would be paralleled is of

a like kind to the new line proposed here.

        The transmission line proposed here is not like the existing line which U3 would parallel.

The existing line is adjacent to Fleming Springs Ranch and discussed in Ms. Jones’s direct

testimony.53 It is roughly 65 feet tall.54 Applicants’ proposed structures will be 140-170 feet tall,

up to potentially 198 feet tall.55 As part of her direct testimony, Ms. Jones photographed the

           A 765-kV transmission line also requires a substantially wider right-of-way corridor than

lower-voltage lines due to the increased tower structure size and mandatory clearance requirements

associated with operating at that voltage. This 765-kV project will require acquisition of new,

independent right-of-way along its corridor, even if it parallels in part the existing line. This further

diminishes the apparent value of Link U3’s paralleling.

          The benefits of paralleling would be in minimizing environmental disturbance, land

fragmentation, and impacts on landowners. These would apply if a new line can share an existing

disturbed corridor. In this case, those benefits do not really exist, because the necessary clearances

and structure footprints of the enormous new line will require the creation of a substantially new

and independent corridor, even when placed near existing infrastructure.

          Further, Route 392’s claimed paralleling advantage diminishes significantly when

examined at the full route level. Route 894 parallels compatible ROW for approximately 98.02

miles of its total 223.17 miles, while Route 392 parallels compatible ROW for approximately 88.46

miles of its total 229.02 miles.56 In other words, when measured in actual ground distance, Route

894 parallels more compatible ROW than Route 392 by nearly 9.6 miles.

                   4. Prudent Avoidance; 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B)(iv)

          Under 16 TAC § 25.101, the Commission is required to follow the policy of prudent

avoidance, which is defined as the “limiting of exposures to electric and magnetic fields that can

be avoided with reasonable investments of money and effort.” 57

          In practical terms, this principle translates to minimizing the number of habitable structures

impacted by the transmission line while controlling costs in a rational and efficient manner.



56
     Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 23 (Combined Data Table).
57

FLEMING SPRINGS INITIAL BRIEF                                                                  PAGE 16
         Route 894 would place 85 habitable structures within 500 feet of the centerline, the third

fewest among all filed routes and 116 fewer than the routes with the highest count. 58 There is not

a single route in the entire proceeding that is cheaper than Route 894 and achieves the same or

fewer habitable structures. Every route with fewer or equal structures costs more. Every route that

costs less has more habitable structures.

        Route 894 crosses 51 fewer habitable structures than Route 392, 44 of which are single-

family residences.59 This is not just a statistic in the EA data; it represents 44 additional homes and

families that would be located within 500 feet of one of the highest-voltage transmission lines in

the State of Texas.

        Prudent avoidance is not only a question of aggregate numbers; it also requires attention to

localized concentrations of impact. Route 392 uses Link E12, a 3.73-mile segment that alone

contains 40 habitable structures.60 This kind of high-concentration is precisely what prudent

avoidance is designed to prevent. When a route alternative exists that avoids this corridor entirely,

as Route 894 does, the Commission’s own framework compels its selection over Route 392.

Approving Route 392 with full knowledge of the residential density along Link E12 would be

difficult to reconcile with any reasonable application of the prudent avoidance standard.

        C. Additional Routing Concerns

        The EA data further supports selection of Route 894 over Route 392 on aviation criteria.

Route 392 passes within 20,000 feet of five FAA-registered airports with runways greater than

3,200 feet in length, compared to only three for Route 894. 61 Route 392 also has one heliport within

          D. Best Route Alternative

          Route 894 respects the community’s long-standing investment in Colorado Bend State Park

and Post Oak Ridge State Park, protects cultural and environmental resources that would otherwise

be placed at risk, performs well with respect to prudent avoidance, and is the lowest-cost route that

meets these objectives. No competing route provides this combination. A side-by-side comparison

associated with operating at that voltage. This 765-kV project will require acquisition of new,

        The benefits of paralleling would be in minimizing environmental disturbance, land

disturbed corridor. In this case, those benefits do not really exist, because the necessary clearances

and structure footprints of the enormous new line will require the creation of a substantially new

and independent corridor, even when placed near existing infrastructure.

examined at the full route level. Route 894 parallels compatible ROW for approximately 98.02

miles ofits total 223.17 miles, while Route 392 parallels compatible ROW for approximately 88.46

894 parallels more compatible ROW than Route 392 by nearly 9.6 miles.


                 4. Prudent Avoidance; 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B)(iv)

        Under 16 TAC § 25.101, the Commission is required to follow the policy of prudent

avoidance, which is defined as the "limiting of exposures to electric and magnetic fields that can

be avoided with reasonable investments of money and effort."57

        In practical terms, this principle translates to minimizing the number ofhabitable structures

impacted by the transmission line while controlling costs in a rational and efficient manner.
